entries.text: Begin with the code we want to write: one ordinary, typed TypeScript method call.
The call happens here, while its implementation can run in a Worker, process, desktop host, or message bus.
The caller simply awaits a Promise whose resolved value is three.
The API shape stays the same even when the implementation runs somewhere else.
JSON R P C is good at defining the request that goes on the wire.
The JSON R P C field identifies the protocol version.
The method field names the operation to invoke.
The params field carries the arguments for that method.
The id correlates this request with exactly one response.
But hand-built requests leak serialization, correlation, dispatch, and deserialization into application code.
TypeScript sees this as plain data, not as a callable API contract shared with the server.
First, a method path is just a string, so a typo like math dot A D survives compilation.
Second, a string can slip into an argument position that should contain a number.
Third, renaming the remote method cannot reliably update string-shaped call sites.
Fourth, every caller must correlate incoming messages with its own pending request.
Fifth, a callback is behavior, so it does not fit the plain JSON value model.
Hard-coded paths hide spelling errors inside strings.
Loose parameter shapes move contract errors from the build into production.
Weak refactors leave breaking changes scattered across call sites.
Correlation and dispatch boilerplate grows again for every method.
Callbacks complete the maintenance problem because functions are not JSON values.
The interface declares that both add arguments are numbers and the result is a Promise of number.
Wrapping the transport with Math A P I brings that contract to the caller.
The string two violates the parameter type, so the TypeScript compiler reports error twenty-three forty-five.
Changing the string to the number two produces the valid call shown below.
A remote breaking change now becomes a local build error before any message travels.
Here the remote download accepts a progress callback as a normal function argument.
The callback receives each progress object from the remote operation.
Application code consumes the percentage exactly where a local callback would.
JSON serialization cannot preserve function behavior; the callback becomes undefined.
K K R P C keeps the function locally under a reference identifier.
Only that reference crosses the transport boundary.
Callback messages route back to the original function, preserving the natural API shape.
K K R P C came from Kunkun's need to keep one API coherent across several very different runtimes.
The Web user interface makes typed calls from a browser surface.
A Rust host owns permissions, process I O, and native capabilities.
Plugins can run in Deno, Node, a Web Worker, or an iframe.
Comlink inspired the proxy-shaped API, but Kunkun needed transports beyond browser endpoints.
On the Worker side, import expose and the self-facing Worker transport.
The Worker API interface describes a nested math object whose add method returns a Promise.
Expose mounts an ordinary object whose real implementation is simply A plus B.
The object's TypeScript shape is the contract.
The transport is supplied separately from that contract.
The implementation stays ordinary TypeScript and never handles message envelopes.
The caller imports wrap, the Worker transport adapter, and the same Worker API type.
It creates a normal platform Worker, with no custom runtime wrapper.
Wrap turns the transport into a proxy typed as Worker A P I.
The application then awaits api dot math dot add exactly like a local call.
Typing api dot now gives editor autocomplete.
The nested math path remains part of the shared contract.
The add arguments and Promise result are checked at the call site.
Begin with the original contract, where the method is named add.
The caller currently invokes that add method.
Now rename the method in the interface from add to sum.
The old call immediately fails because add no longer exists on the typed contract.
The updated interface now exposes sum as the supported method.
An editor rename updates the caller to api dot math dot sum.
Keep three layers separate: the Proxy, the Channel, and the Transport.
The Proxy records property paths, arguments, and remote references.
The Channel owns request identifiers, pending Promises, timeouts, and dispatch.
The Transport only needs to send, receive, and close.
Because those boundaries are clean, change the transport without changing the API.
Follow api dot math dot add from the typed Proxy to the remote boundary.
The Proxy records the property path math dot add and the call arguments.
The Channel allocates an id and stores the Promise resolver in its pending map.
The Transport sends the compact request while the local Promise waits.
The visible record carries a request tag, id, path, and argument array.
On the remote side, the transport delivers that request to the exposed API.
The exposed object locates add and evaluates one plus two.
The result is wrapped in a response carrying the same request id.
Back at the caller, the Channel finds the waiting resolver and fulfills the Promise with three.
It also clears the timeout and deletes the completed pending entry.
The core wire protocol uses small request and response records with explicit lifecycle messages.
The id field links the request on the left to the response on the right.
The P field carries the nested property path.
The A field carries the call's argument array.
The V field contains the returned value, while errors use the corresponding error shape.
References, callback invocations, and releases add explicit cleanup paths around the remote API.
Browser boundaries include Web Workers, iframes, and Chrome extensions.
Process boundaries can use framed standard input and output.
Network adapters include H T T P, WebSocket, Hono, Elysia, and Socket I O.
Desktop applications can cross Electron and Tauri boundaries.
Event-bus adapters cover Rabbit M Q, Kafka, Redis Streams, and NATS.
Fifteen adapters are visible, yet application code keeps one typed call surface.
One API shape does not erase the physical capabilities of each transport.
H T T P is fundamentally unary request and response.
Workers and iframes can use structured clone and transferable objects.
WebSocket and Socket I O naturally support duplex connections and remote references.
Standard I O must handle process lifecycle and message framing.
Event buses add subjects, consumers, delivery rules, and broadcast semantics.
Object mode avoids forced JSON serialization where the runtime already moves objects safely.
Choose an adapter by the capability you need, not by its logo.
Middleware wraps the R P C boundary so logging, authorization, timing, and policy stay out of business methods.
The interceptor first records the start time from the performance clock.
Awaiting next enters the inner handler and the remaining onion layers.
After the call returns, the interceptor logs the method and elapsed time, then returns the result.
Before next, middleware can inspect and modify the call context.
The highlighted next call enters the middleware onion exactly once.
After next resolves, the outer layer can observe either the result or the error.
Static types protect compiled code, while Standard Schema validators protect values that arrive at runtime.
The input schema requires a tuple containing two numbers.
The output schema requires the implementation to return a number.
Malformed input is rejected before the implementation executes.
Output validation verifies the implementation side of the same runtime contract.
Opt into schemas at trust boundaries instead of imposing them on every call.
The small core combines a typed nested API with fifteen swappable transports.
Add callback references when functions must cross the boundary.
Add streaming when values need a lifecycle beyond one response.
Add middleware for cross-cutting policy around the handler.
Add schema validation where runtime inputs and outputs are not already trusted.
Every optional capability still fits the same mental model: Proxy, Channel, Transport.
JSON R P C, Comlink, and K K R P C solve related problems at different scopes.
JSON R P C is a language-neutral wire protocol, and generated clients can add a typed surface.
Comlink provides excellent proxy ergonomics for browser ports and remote references.
K K R P C extends a native typed proxy across adapter-based runtimes, with optional validation and middleware.
Choose JSON R P C when a simple, language-neutral protocol is the central requirement.
Choose Comlink when the browser boundary and its concise R P C ergonomics are exactly the scope you need.
Use K K R P C when the API should remain stable even as the transport changes.
The typed API gives autocomplete, safe refactors, and local build errors.
The Channel manages request, callback, and stream lifecycles.
The adapter is chosen for the Worker, process, desktop host, plugin, network, or event bus you actually have.
The application sees one typed call. Another runtime performs the work.
Start by installing K K R P C from N P M, or from J S R when using Deno.
The documentation covers each adapter and optional capability.
The source code, issues, and examples live in the Kunkun S H repository on GitHub.
The package is published today as K K R P C.
